Much spatial data arrives as rasters (gridded images such as elevation or
climate) or as polygons (such as countries or study areas). This vignette shows
how to move both onto globalhex cells. It uses the
[terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/),
[exactextractr](https://isciences.gitlab.io/exactextractr/), and
[sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) packages.

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(globalhex)
library(terra)
```

## From raster to cells

terra includes a small elevation raster of Luxembourg:

```{r}
elevation <- rast(system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra"))
elevation
```

`raster_to_cell()` finds every cell that overlaps the raster and summarizes the
pixels inside each one:

```{r}
elevation_hex <- raster_to_cell(elevation, resolution = 8, progress = FALSE)
elevation_hex

plot(elevation_hex)
```

The result is a `hex_data` object, so everything in `vignette("plotting")`
applies. Cells where the raster has no data are dropped; use `drop_na = FALSE`
to keep them.

### How pixels are summarized

By default, each cell gets the **area-weighted mean** of the pixels it overlaps.
A pixel that is only partly inside a cell counts only for the part inside. Area
weighting matters for longitude/latitude rasters, whose pixels get smaller
toward the poles. For categorical rasters, such as land cover, the default is
the most common class, weighted the same way.

Choose other summaries with `fun`, using any
[exactextractr summary](https://isciences.gitlab.io/exactextractr/reference/exact_extract.html):

```{r}
elevation_range <- raster_to_cell(
  elevation,
  resolution = 7,
  fun = c("min", "max"),
  progress = FALSE
)
elevation_range
```

Set `weights = NULL` to weight pixels only by how much of each one falls inside
the cell, without accounting for pixel area.

## Into cells you already have

If you already have cells, perhaps from binning points, bring raster values
into them with one of two functions:

- `cell_extract()` uses the same exact, area-weighted summaries as
  `raster_to_cell()`.
- `cell_sample()` reads the single pixel under each cell's center. It is much
  faster but ignores the rest of the cell, so it suits rasters whose pixels are
  smaller than the cells.

```{r}
sites <- point_to_cell(
  data.frame(lon = c(6.13, 5.97, 6.36), lat = c(49.61, 49.90, 49.75)),
  resolution = 7
)

cell_extract(sites, elevation)
cell_sample(sites, elevation)
```

## Rasters that cover the globe

Global rasters work the same way. Rasters whose longitudes run from 0 to 360,
or that use a projected coordinate system, are handled automatically. A global
grid has many cells at fine resolutions (see the table in
`vignette("globalhex")`), so `raster_to_cell()` stops with an error if a result
would exceed `max_cells`. Raise it deliberately when you need more.

## From polygons to cells

`cell_cover()` returns the cells whose **centers** fall inside a polygon:

```{r}
counties <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
county <- counties[counties$NAME == "Wake", ]

wake_cells <- cell_cover(county, resolution = 8)
length(wake_cells)
```

```{r}
plot(sf::st_geometry(county), border = "black", lwd = 2)
plot(sf::st_geometry(sf::st_as_sf(wake_cells)), add = TRUE, border = "steelblue")
```

Because selection is by cell center, cells along the edge may stick out of the
polygon or leave small gaps. Use a finer resolution to follow the edge more
closely.

Holes in polygons, such as a lake inside a park, are excluded by default; set
`include_holes = FALSE` to ignore them. Large polygons at fine resolutions can
produce a great many cells, so `cell_cover()` also has a `max_cells` limit.

## Back to sf

To combine cells with other vector data, convert them to sf polygons with
`sf::st_as_sf()`. Each row is one cell:

```{r}
sf::st_as_sf(wake_cells[1:3])
```
